items.prompt: At Jefferson Middle School, the stopwatch showed 8 seconds per student paying at the register and 40 seconds per student deciding what to take. If the school buys a second register, what happens to the 24-minute line?
choices: It's cut roughly in half, since the register step that took 8 seconds per student now runs twice as fast with two lines open
It barely changes, because checkout was never the bottleneck — students still stall at the food station
It gets noticeably worse, because two separate registers end up confusing students about which line to actually join
It disappears entirely once any visible change is made, since students assume management has already fixed the problem
items.explanation: A second register only speeds up the 8-second step. The 40-second decision step at the food station is untouched, so the line still stalls there — the fix targeted the wrong stage of the process.
items.reference:
StepSeconds/student
Paying at register8
Deciding at food station40

Why: a fix only helps if it targets the step that's actually the bottleneck — speeding up a fast step does almost nothing.

items.prompt: Why did watching the line for ten minutes matter more than the principal's first instinct ('buy a second register')?
choices: Watching is always the more expensive option to run, so it mainly signals to parents that the school takes the problem seriously
It revealed where the actual delay was happening (deciding, not paying), which the principal's instinct had guessed wrong
It didn't really matter either way — the principal's register instinct turned out to be exactly correct once tested
Watching is only useful after a first fix has already been tried and has clearly failed to solve the problem
items.explanation: The principal's instinct assumed the register was the bottleneck without checking. Ten minutes of direct observation found the real bottleneck was decision time at the food station — a fact no amount of guessing would have surfaced.
items.reference:
StepSeconds/student
Paying at register8
Deciding at food station40

Why: a fix only helps if it targets the step that's actually the bottleneck — speeding up a fast step does almost nothing.

items.prompt: What are the five stages of design thinking, in order?
choices: Define, Empathize, Prototype, Ideate, Test — starting from naming the problem before anyone has observed it
Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
Ideate, Empathize, Test, Define, Prototype — generating ideas before any observation has happened at all
Empathize, Prototype, Define, Test, Ideate — building something real before the problem itself is even named
items.explanation: The sequence is Empathize (observe), Define (name the real problem), Ideate (generate many candidate solutions), Prototype (build a cheap test), Test (watch what real people do with it).
items.reference:
① Empathize
② Define
③ Ideate
④ Prototype
⑤ Test

Why: each stage's output feeds the next — Ideate can't run without a Define statement to ideate against.

items.prompt: Which stage comes right before Prototype?
choices: Empathize, since observing comes before any idea is generated or built
Define
Ideate
Test
items.explanation: Ideate generates the range of candidate solutions; Prototype takes one of those candidates and builds the cheapest version that can test it. You can't meaningfully prototype before you have ideas to choose from.
items.reference:
① Empathize
② Define
③ Ideate
④ Prototype
⑤ Test

Why: each stage's output feeds the next — Ideate can't run without a Define statement to ideate against.

items.prompt: A team writes a specific, human-centered problem statement before generating any candidate solutions. Which two stages does that describe, in order?
choices: Ideate, then Define
Empathize, then Test
Define, then Ideate
Prototype, then Ideate
items.explanation: Writing the problem statement is Define; generating candidate solutions against that statement is Ideate. Define always precedes Ideate — you need a defined problem before you can meaningfully brainstorm solutions to it.
items.reference:
① Empathize
② Define
③ Ideate
④ Prototype
⑤ Test

Why: each stage's output feeds the next — Ideate can't run without a Define statement to ideate against.

items.prompt: A team finishes Test, and the paper menu board works. Two weeks later, the register develops a new stall for a different reason. What does design thinking say to do?
choices: Nothing — the five stages were already completed once for the original problem, so the process is permanently done
Re-enter the loop for the new symptom, starting with Empathize on that specific stall
Skip straight to a new Prototype, since the team already knows the five stages well enough to not repeat them
Ignore the new stall entirely, since only the original decision-time problem was ever officially in scope
items.explanation: Design thinking is a loop, not a one-time checklist. A new symptom is a signal to re-enter the cycle for that specific problem, starting with observation — not to assume the team's existing familiarity with the stages substitutes for actually looking at the new stall.
items.reference:
🔁 A finished pass doesn't retire the loop — a new symptom re-enters it.

Why: design thinking is iterative by design — each new finding can send you back to an earlier stage.

items.prompt: Why is design thinking usually drawn as a loop with arrows going backward, instead of a straight line from Empathize to Test?
choices: Because a looping diagram simply looks more visually interesting to stakeholders than a plain straight line would
Because a Test finding can reveal the problem was framed wrong or a group was missed entirely, which sends you back to an earlier stage rather than forward
Because Empathize and Test are actually the exact same activity, just performed at two different points in time
Because the five stages have to be mechanically repeated in a fixed cycle no matter what Test actually finds
items.explanation: The backward arrows represent real information flow: what you learn from Test can invalidate an earlier stage's output (a wrong Define statement, a missed group during Empathize), which is exactly when you loop back — not out of habit, but because the finding demands it.
items.reference:
🔁 A finished pass doesn't retire the loop — a new symptom re-enters it.

Why: design thinking is iterative by design — each new finding can send you back to an earlier stage.

items.prompt: Which of these counts as genuine Empathize work, rather than guessing dressed up as research?
choices: Writing down what you personally assume students find most annoying about standing in that long lunch line
Watching the actual line for ten minutes with a stopwatch, before proposing any fix
Asking the principal directly what they personally think the real underlying problem with the line is
Reviewing last year's cafeteria budget report for clues about where money was spent on the lunch line
items.explanation: Empathize means directly observing or talking to the people who have the problem. Watching the real line with a stopwatch produces direct evidence; personal assumptions, secondhand opinions, and unrelated documents don't.
items.reference:
Assuming

Guessing from your own experience or someone's opinion

Empathizing

Directly observing or talking to the people with the problem

Why: Empathize specifically means direct contact with the problem, not secondhand opinion about it.

items.prompt: A team writes a three-question survey about the cafeteria line before anyone has watched it in person. What's the risk?
choices: None at all — a well-written survey is always functionally equivalent to watching the real line in person
The survey's questions were written from assumptions about the problem, so it can only confirm or deny those assumptions, not surface a friction point nobody thought to ask about
Surveys are only ever useful once a population is large enough, which doesn't apply to a single school cafeteria
Surveys simply take longer to run than direct observation does, so they should basically never be used at all
items.explanation: A survey written before anyone observed the real behavior can only test the assumptions baked into its questions. It can't catch something like the 40-second decision stall unless someone already suspected to ask about it — direct observation catches what nobody thought to ask.
items.reference:
Assuming

Guessing from your own experience or someone's opinion

Empathizing

Directly observing or talking to the people with the problem

Why: Empathize specifically means direct contact with the problem, not secondhand opinion about it.

items.prompt: What's the core difference between Empathize and simply trusting your own experience of a problem?
choices: There is no real difference at all — your own personal experience already counts as a valid form of Empathize
Empathize requires observing or talking to the actual people affected, since your own experience may not represent theirs at all
Empathize is only ever about reading through existing complaint tickets that students have already filed
Empathize simply means going and asking managers what they personally believe the underlying problem actually is
items.explanation: Your own experience is one data point, and often an unrepresentative one — the person designing a fix is rarely the person most affected by the problem. Empathize means going to the actual affected people, not substituting your own assumptions for their reality.
items.reference:
Assuming

Guessing from your own experience or someone's opinion

Empathizing

Directly observing or talking to the people with the problem

Why: Empathize specifically means direct contact with the problem, not secondhand opinion about it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a proper Define statement, and which is a solution wearing a problem's clothes?
choices: "We need a second register" is the Define statement; "kids stall deciding what to eat" is actually the solution
"Kids stall deciding what to eat" is the Define statement; "we need a second register" already assumes a fix
Both statements are equally valid, interchangeable Define statements that could be written down in either order
Neither one is a valid Define statement at all — only a formal survey result ever counts as a real one
items.explanation: "Kids stall deciding what to eat" names the actual human-centered problem with no fix implied. "We need a second register" names a specific solution, which forecloses considering any other fix before Ideate even starts.
items.reference:
Solution in disguise

"We need a second register"

Real problem statement

"Kids stall deciding what to eat"

Why: a Define statement that names a fix has already skipped Ideate before it started.

items.prompt: Why is "we need a second register" a weak thing to write down at the Define stage?
choices: Because it happens to be factually wrong in literally every cafeteria that has ever tried adding a second register
Because it already commits to a specific fix, leaving Ideate nothing left to generate but variations on that one fix
Because a second register is always, in every case, more expensive to install than any other possible fix
Because Define statements are only ever supposed to describe feelings and emotions, never concrete facts
items.explanation: A Define statement's job is to leave the solution space open. Naming a specific fix (a register) collapses that space before Ideate has a chance to generate other candidates, some of which — like a menu board — might work better and cost far less.
items.reference:
Solution in disguise

"We need a second register"

Real problem statement

"Kids stall deciding what to eat"

Why: a Define statement that names a fix has already skipped Ideate before it started.

items.prompt: A teammate says, "our Define statement is 'add a menu board' — let's move to Ideate." What's the problem with moving forward like that?
choices: There's no problem at all with that — "add a menu board" is a perfectly good, properly-scoped Define statement
It's already a solution, not a problem statement, so Ideate would just be generating variations of a menu board instead of exploring the actual range of possible fixes
Menu boards specifically are never a valid fix for any kind of cafeteria line problem, under any circumstance
Define statements are supposed to be written as exactly one single word, with no additional context at all
items.explanation: "Add a menu board" is already an idea, not a problem statement — it belongs at Ideate or later, not at Define. Moving forward with it as Define skips the step where other, possibly better ideas could have been generated.
items.reference:
Solution in disguise

"We need a second register"

Real problem statement

"Kids stall deciding what to eat"

Why: a Define statement that names a fix has already skipped Ideate before it started.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly fills the Define statement shape: "[Person/group] needs a way to [do something] because [underlying reason]"?
choices: "Students need a bigger, brighter menu board because the current sign is too small and hard to read from the line"
"Students at the food station need a way to decide what to take before reaching the counter, because deciding under time pressure with a line behind them causes the stall"
"The cafeteria needs a second register installed because the current checkout line is simply taking too long"
"The school needs to hire an outside design agency because several parents have been complaining about the wait"
items.explanation: The correct statement names the underlying mechanism (deciding under time pressure) without naming any specific fix. The others each smuggle in a solution — a board, a register, an agency — before Ideate has had a chance to run.
items.reference:
[Person/group] needs a way to [do something] because [underlying reason, not the requested item].

Why: this shape structurally can't contain a solution — it forces the reason, not the fix, into the sentence.

items.prompt: What's the actual purpose of writing a Define statement in the "[who] needs a way to [what] because [why]" shape, instead of just describing the complaint directly?
choices: It makes the resulting statement noticeably longer, which signals to reviewers that more real effort went into writing it
It forces the underlying reason into words, which structurally prevents a specific fix from being named as the 'problem'
It's purely a stylistic formatting convention, chosen for readability, with no real functional purpose behind it
It guarantees that whatever idea eventually comes out of Ideate will be cheap and fast for the team to build
items.explanation: The shape's power is structural: filling in "because [reason]" forces you to articulate the underlying mechanism, and that slot has no room for a solution noun. A complaint restated directly ("the form is ugly") can smuggle in a fix; this shape resists it.
items.reference:
[Person/group] needs a way to [do something] because [underlying reason, not the requested item].

Why: this shape structurally can't contain a solution — it forces the reason, not the fix, into the sentence.

items.prompt: A statement reads: "Employees need a more modern, visually appealing expense form." What test quickly shows this is a weak Define statement?
choices: Check whether the sentence is grammatically correct as written — it clearly is, so by that measure it's fine
Check whether it names a specific artifact or feature (it does: "a form") — a real Define statement should be answerable by many different kinds of ideas, not just variations on one
Check whether the employees themselves agree with the statement — if they do, it's automatically a strong one
Check its total word count against a fixed rule — real Define statements are required to stay under ten words
items.explanation: Naming a specific artifact ("a form") means every subsequent idea can only be a variation on that artifact's design. A strong Define statement should be open enough that Ideate could reasonably propose completely different kinds of fixes.
items.reference:
[Person/group] needs a way to [do something] because [underlying reason, not the requested item].

Why: this shape structurally can't contain a solution — it forces the reason, not the fix, into the sentence.

items.prompt: During a brainstorm, a facilitator asks for twenty ideas and bans the word "no" for fifteen minutes. What is this protecting against?
choices: Nothing in particular — it's really just meant as a fun icebreaker exercise to loosen the room up before working
Judging ideas while generating them, which tends to collapse the search to whatever's already familiar instead of exploring a wider range
Running out of available time before the team can even get to the Prototype stage of the process
Letting quieter team members contribute more — a facilitation goal unrelated to judgment during idea generation
items.explanation: Judgment applied during generation narrows the search early, usually toward the first familiar idea. Deferring judgment (the divergent half of Ideate) widens the net before the convergent half narrows it back down with explicit criteria.
items.reference:
HalfRule
DivergentQuantity first, defer judgment
ConvergentApply judgment, narrow with stated criteria

Why: judging while generating collapses the search early — the two halves are kept separate on purpose.

items.prompt: A group picks its favorite idea five minutes into a brainstorm and stops generating more. What did they skip?
choices: Nothing really — picking a clear favorite early on just means the brainstorming process was unusually efficient
The rest of the divergent half — deferring judgment long enough to reach ideas beyond the first obvious ones, some of which tend to be the strongest
The Prototype stage, which the group should technically have run before ever starting to Ideate in the first place
The Empathize stage, since in their view ideas should always be generated before anyone observes real users
items.explanation: Picking a favorite five minutes in ends the divergent half before it's done its job. The first ideas in any session tend to be small variations on the obvious fix; reaching further, past the easy answers, is where the strongest ideas tend to surface.
items.reference:
HalfRule
DivergentQuantity first, defer judgment
ConvergentApply judgment, narrow with stated criteria

Why: judging while generating collapses the search early — the two halves are kept separate on purpose.

items.prompt: What's the difference between the divergent and convergent halves of Ideate?
choices: Divergent happens only after Prototype is finished; convergent happens only before Empathize has even started
Divergent generates a wide range of ideas while deferring judgment; convergent groups, votes, and narrows that range using stated criteria
Divergent is always done entirely alone by one person; convergent is always done together as a full group
There's no real difference between the two at all — both halves ultimately mean the exact same thing in practice
items.explanation: Divergent widens the pool of candidate ideas without judging any of them yet; convergent then applies explicit criteria to narrow that pool to a short list worth prototyping. Doing them in the wrong order (judging while generating) collapses the search early.
items.reference:
HalfRule
DivergentQuantity first, defer judgment
ConvergentApply judgment, narrow with stated criteria

Why: judging while generating collapses the search early — the two halves are kept separate on purpose.

items.prompt: The cafeteria team picks "a menu board with photos, grouped by prep time" as its idea. Should they hire a sign shop before testing it?
choices: Yes — a finished, professionally made sign is always the correct first version of any idea worth testing at all
No — a rough paper version taped up for one lunch period tests the same core assumption at a fraction of the cost of being wrong
No — the idea should be abandoned outright instead of being tested in any form, cheap or otherwise
Yes, but only if the school's budget happens to comfortably allow for a professional sign shop this quarter
items.explanation: A finished artifact is expensive to change if the idea turns out wrong. A Prototype only needs to be real enough to test the riskiest assumption — here, whether a visible board shortens decision time at all — which a taped-up sheet of paper can test just as validly.
items.reference:
🧻 Paper sign

Cheap, fast, disposable if wrong

🪧 Laminated sign

Expensive, slow, costly if wrong

Why: a Prototype only needs to be real enough to test the riskiest assumption, not finished.

items.prompt: What defines a good Prototype, according to the model?
choices: The most polished, production-ready version of the idea that the team can realistically afford to build right now
The cheapest, roughest artifact that can still test the riskiest assumption behind the idea
Whatever version simply takes the least amount of time to build, regardless of whether it actually tests anything useful
A version that ends up being essentially identical to whatever the team eventually plans to ship for real
items.explanation: A Prototype's job is to test an assumption cheaply before committing real resources, not to be a near-final product. "Cheapest version that still tests the risky part" is the actual bar — polish and completeness are explicitly not the goal at this stage.
items.reference:
🧻 Paper sign

Cheap, fast, disposable if wrong

🪧 Laminated sign

Expensive, slow, costly if wrong

Why: a Prototype only needs to be real enough to test the riskiest assumption, not finished.

items.prompt: After putting up the paper menu board, which is the stronger form of Test?
choices: Asking students casually in the hallway afterward, "hey, did you like the new sign we put up by the register?"
Timing the real line with the paper board up and comparing it to the earlier baseline
Asking the principal directly whether they personally think the new sign looks good enough to keep around
Counting how many students glanced at the sign at all, with no regard for what happened to their actual line time
items.explanation: The Define statement was about decision time, so the direct test is measuring decision time with the prototype in place. A reported opinion ("did you like it?") doesn't measure the thing the problem statement was actually about.
items.reference:
Asked opinion

"Did you like the sign?"

Measured behavior

Stopwatch reading with the board up

Why: Test should measure the actual behavior the Define statement was about, not a reported opinion about the artifact.

items.prompt: Why is a stopwatch reading treated as stronger evidence than "students said they liked the sign"?
choices: Because stopwatches as instruments are more expensive to buy than paper surveys, so the resulting data must be better
Because it directly measures the behavior the Define statement was actually about, while a reported opinion can diverge from what someone actually does
Because students, as a general rule, always lie when answering any kind of survey question about the cafeteria
There's no real difference between the two at all — both forms of evidence carry exactly equal weight either way
items.explanation: "Liking" a sign and having your decision time actually change are two different things. A stopwatch reading measures the exact mechanism named in the Define statement; a reported opinion is one step removed and can disagree with the measured behavior.
items.reference:
Asked opinion

"Did you like the sign?"

Measured behavior

Stopwatch reading with the board up

Why: Test should measure the actual behavior the Define statement was about, not a reported opinion about the artifact.

items.prompt: A team's only evidence for a successful Test is "users said they liked the prototype." What's missing?
choices: Nothing at all — a clearly positive stated opinion from users is already sufficient evidence of real success here
Observed behavior — a measurement of what people actually did with the prototype, since stated preference and actual behavior can diverge
Simply a bigger sample size of that exact same kind of stated opinion, collected from more students over more days
Formal sign-off and approval from someone senior on the team, confirming the result looks good enough to ship
items.explanation: "They said they liked it" is opinion evidence, which the model treats as weaker than behavior evidence. Test is meant to observe what people actually do with the prototype — the two can disagree even when asked of the very same person.
items.reference:
Asked opinion

"Did you like the sign?"

Measured behavior

Stopwatch reading with the board up

Why: Test should measure the actual behavior the Define statement was about, not a reported opinion about the artifact.

items.prompt: A Test shows the menu board's wording confused students, even though a visible board clearly reduced hesitation overall. Which stage should the team loop back to?
choices: Empathize, since a confusing result like this must mean an entirely new group of students was missed in research
Define, since a confused reaction to the wording must mean the entire original problem was framed wrong from the start
Prototype, since the underlying concept works and only the execution needs another pass
None — a confusing result like this one means the whole project should simply be cancelled outright
items.explanation: The concept (a visible board reduces hesitation) was validated; only the wording's execution failed. That's a signal to refine the Prototype, not to reopen Define or Empathize, which would be re-litigating something the test already confirmed.
items.reference:
Test resultLoop back to

Board's wording confuses, concept still soundPrototype
Kids read fine but stall on price, not menuDefine

Why: which stage you loop back to depends on what kind of surprise the test produced, not on a fixed rule.

items.prompt: A Test shows students read the new board just fine, but still stall in line — because they're now comparing prices, not menu items. Which stage should the team loop back to, and why?
choices: Prototype, since the board's visual design and layout must be the actual thing causing students to compare prices
Define, since the real problem was named wrong — it's price anxiety, not menu confusion
Test, since the exact same test should simply be run again, unchanged, to see if the same result repeats
No loop needed at all — the original fix is already close enough to acceptable as currently built
items.explanation: The prototype executed the original idea correctly, and it still didn't work — that's a sign the problem itself was framed wrong, not that the artifact needs polishing. That calls for a new Define statement (price anxiety), not another pass at the same Prototype.
items.reference:
Test resultLoop back to

Why: which stage you loop back to depends on what kind of surprise the test produced, not on a fixed rule.

Employees struggled to accurately recall purchase details after batching receipts for weeks before filing, which the survey's framing never captured
Employees didn't understand how the company's expense reporting process worked at all, from start to finish
There was no real friction anywhere in the process — the original survey complaint turned out to be entirely baseless

That's a fixable process gap, not a character judgment about employees — and it only surfaced through observation of her actual rejection pattern.

items.prompt: Why did the team shadow six employees across different roles (frequent travelers, a rare filer, an approver) instead of just watching one person file one report?
choices: To make the eventual research write-up look more thorough and rigorous once it's presented to leadership later

Because written company policy specifically requires shadowing at least six separate employees before any redesign
It didn't really matter either way — one single person's experience would have been just as informative overall

items.prompt: Instead of building OCR receipt-scanning, the team tested with a shared spreadsheet and a person manually logging texted photos. What kind of prototype is this?
choices: A fully finished production feature, essentially the real OCR system, just quietly deployed without anyone noticing
A Wizard of Oz prototype — a human manually performs what the eventual software would automate, to test the underlying assumption cheaply
Not a valid prototype of any kind at all, since no actual code or engineering work was involved in building it
A focus group exercise rather than a prototype, since it mainly involved people talking about the idea out loud
items.explanation: A Wizard of Oz prototype uses a human to simulate automated behavior, letting the team test whether the underlying idea (moment-of-purchase logging) works before investing in the actual automation. It's a legitimate, and often the cheapest, form of prototype.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Wizard of Oz

A human manually does what software would automate — cheap, fast to change

🤖 Full OCR build

Real automation — expensive, slow to change if wrong

Why: a Wizard of Oz prototype tests the underlying assumption without paying the cost of building the real automation first.

items.prompt: OCR receipt-scanning tested as the most exciting idea in the brainstorm. Why did the team prototype the spreadsheet-plus-human version first instead?
choices: Because building real OCR receipt-scanning is technically impossible with the tools and vendors available right now

Because the spreadsheet version tests the same underlying assumption — that moment-of-purchase logging improves accuracy — at a fraction of the cost, without also risking failure from unrelated causes like OCR misreads
Because a plain spreadsheet is, as a general rule, always superior to any properly coded and engineered feature
Because the team had already privately decided OCR was a bad idea well before testing anything about it at all
items.explanation: Building OCR first would have tested the core assumption indirectly, wrapped inside a feature that could also fail for reasons unrelated to the assumption itself, like poor photo quality. The cheap prototype isolates and tests just the assumption that actually mattered.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Wizard of Oz

A human manually does what software would automate — cheap, fast to change

🤖 Full OCR build

Real automation — expensive, slow to change if wrong

Why: a Wizard of Oz prototype tests the underlying assumption without paying the cost of building the real automation first.

items.prompt: What was the "riskiest assumption" the ExpenseFlow team needed to test before writing any code?
choices: Whether employees would personally prefer a blue or a green color scheme for the new expense-reporting interface
Whether logging expenses at the moment of purchase, instead of batching them later, would actually improve filing accuracy
Whether the company could realistically afford to pay for an outside design agency to rebuild the whole app
Whether reliable OCR software even exists anywhere that's capable of accurately reading a crumpled paper receipt
items.explanation: The Define statement's core claim was that moment-of-purchase logging closes the accuracy gap caused by delayed, batched filing. That's the assumption the Wizard of Oz test targeted directly, before any engineering investment in a specific implementation.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Wizard of Oz

A human manually does what software would automate — cheap, fast to change

🤖 Full OCR build

Real automation — expensive, slow to change if wrong

Why: a Wizard of Oz prototype tests the underlying assumption without paying the cost of building the real automation first.

items.prompt: Which of these is the failure mode ExpenseFlow's product lead almost committed on day one?
choices: Spending far too long stuck in Empathize mode, endlessly observing employees without ever shipping anything at all
Skipping straight from a complaint ("outdated UI") to Prototype, by hiring a design agency before anyone had watched real filing behavior
Generating far too many candidate ideas during the Ideate stage, overwhelming the team with too many options
Testing the prototype with far too many volunteers, making the resulting Test data harder to interpret cleanly
items.explanation: Hiring the agency immediately after the survey would have jumped from complaint straight to Prototype, skipping Empathize and Define entirely — shipping a modernized version of the same broken workflow, since the underlying friction (categorizing weeks-old receipts) was never touched.
items.reference:
⚠️ Skipping straight to Prototype
⚠️ A Define statement that already names the fix
⚠️ Prototyping the flashiest idea, not the cheapest test
⚠️ Grading Test on opinions instead of behavior

Why: each of these failure modes skips exactly the protection that stage was supposed to provide.

items.prompt: Three of five volunteers said the new process "felt about the same," even though their filing timestamps showed real improvement. What failure would the team have committed by trusting only their comments?
choices: Skipping the Ideate stage entirely and jumping straight from Define to building a Prototype without any ideas
Grading Test on stated opinions instead of the actual behavior the Define statement was about
Building a Prototype that ended up being far too expensive and polished for what the team actually needed to test
Choosing the wrong Define statement from the very start, before any Prototype or Test had even been run yet
items.explanation: Self-reported opinion ("felt about the same") and measured behavior (timestamps) disagreed here. Grading Test on the opinion alone would have missed a real, measured improvement — exactly the failure mode of trusting stated preference over observed behavior.

⚠️ Skipping straight to Prototype
⚠️ A Define statement that already names the fix
⚠️ Prototyping the flashiest idea, not the cheapest test
⚠️ Grading Test on opinions instead of behavior

Why: each of these failure modes skips exactly the protection that stage was supposed to provide.

items.prompt: OCR receipt-scanning was the flashiest idea from Ideate. Building it first, before testing the cheaper Wizard of Oz version, would have been an example of which failure mode?
choices: Skipping the Define stage entirely and jumping straight from a vague complaint directly into building something
Prototyping the most exciting idea instead of the cheapest way to test the assumption underneath it
Not generating a wide enough range of candidate ideas during the Ideate stage before picking one to prototype
Failing to actually observe real users carefully enough during the earlier Empathize stage of the process
items.explanation: Choosing to build the flashiest idea (OCR) first, rather than the cheapest test of the shared underlying assumption, would have spent real engineering time learning something a spreadsheet could have validated for free — the specific failure mode named in this unit.

items.prompt: According to the unit, when is running the full five-stage design thinking cycle actually overkill?
choices: Whenever the problem happens to involve more than one single stakeholder weighing in on the final decision
For a well-understood problem with clear precedent, like fixing a known typo or a broken link — there's no real ambiguity about the problem left to uncover
Whenever the eventual fix will take the engineering team more than a single day of work to actually build
The full five-stage cycle is never overkill in any situation at all, regardless of how well-understood the problem is
items.explanation: The loop exists to resolve genuine uncertainty about the problem. When there's no ambiguity left — a known typo, a broken link — running the full ceremony formalizes a decision that was never actually in doubt, which is its own failure mode.
items.reference:
Full cycle warranted

High uncertainty, many stakeholders, expensive to reverse

Overkill

Well-understood problem, clear precedent

Why: the loop resolves real uncertainty about the problem — running it where none exists formalizes a decision that was never in doubt.

items.prompt: If ExpenseFlow were a customer-facing product used by thousands of people instead of an internal tool used by dozens, what does the unit say about running the full cycle?
choices: It would actually matter less in that case, since customer-facing products tend to be inherently simpler to design for
It becomes close to mandatory — the cost of empathizing wrong is multiplied by the scale of who's affected
The full cycle should instead be skipped entirely in that case, purely to help the team move faster for customers
Scale has essentially no real bearing on whether running the full cycle is worth the team's time and effort
items.explanation: Higher stakes and larger scale raise the cost of getting Empathize or Define wrong — a mistaken problem statement now misleads a much bigger build. That's exactly the situation where investing in the full cycle pays for itself.
items.reference:

High uncertainty, many stakeholders, expensive to reverse

Overkill

Well-understood problem, clear precedent

Why: the loop resolves real uncertainty about the problem — running it where none exists formalizes a decision that was never in doubt.

items.prompt: A trivial internal change has exactly one user and takes five minutes to build. Does design thinking's underlying loop still apply?
choices: No — design thinking as a practice only ever applies to large, expensive, multi-team projects, never small ones
Conceptually yes, just heavily compressed — a quick conversation can substitute for formal Empathize/Define when the stakes and uncertainty are both this low
Yes, and the full multi-week formal research process is still fully required here regardless of how low the stakes are
No — in a case this small, the change should simply be made without ever talking to the one affected user at all
items.explanation: The underlying logic (understand before building) still applies, but its ceremony scales with uncertainty and stakes, not with a fixed process length. A five-minute conversation with the one affected user can serve the same role Empathize/Define serve at larger scale.

Overkill

Well-understood problem, clear precedent

Why: the loop resolves real uncertainty about the problem — running it where none exists formalizes a decision that was never in doubt.

items.prompt: The Test found that reps still resisted logging cash purchases, since there was no receipt photo to trigger the process. What should the team do with that finding?
choices: Treat it as definitive proof that the entire redesign failed outright, and restart the whole project completely from scratch
Treat it as a new, narrower Empathize question for a follow-up loop, since it's a distinct sub-problem the current fix wasn't scoped to solve
Ignore the finding entirely, since the core metrics the team already cared about — same-day filing, rejection rate — already improved
Quietly fold it into the existing fix without running any further observation or research on the cash-purchase behavior at all
items.explanation: The cash-purchase gap is a genuinely new finding, distinct from the delayed-filing problem the current loop solved. The right response is a fresh, narrowly-scoped Empathize pass on that specific sub-problem — not restarting everything, and not silently patching it without observation.
items.reference:
🔍 New finding: cash purchases have no photo trigger
➡️ Narrow re-loop: new Empathize for that sub-problem
🚫 Not: restart the whole project

Why: a new finding scopes a fresh, narrow loop — it doesn't invalidate the parts of the process that already succeeded.

items.prompt: Angela's category-mismatch problem was deliberately kept as its own separate loop instead of being folded into the receipt-timing fix. Why?
choices: Because problems that originate on the approver's side of the process are never considered worth solving by the team

Because it's a genuinely distinct problem with its own root cause (label mismatch, not filing delay) — solving both with one Define statement risks a fix that half-addresses each and fully solves neither
Because Angela's specific role as an approver doesn't meaningfully matter to the overall success of the project
Because the team had simply run out of available time to properly investigate her particular problem at all
items.explanation: Bundling two distinct root causes into one Define statement tends to produce a fix that's a compromise between two different problems, addressing neither well. Keeping them as separate loops let each get a Define statement and Prototype actually aimed at its own cause.
items.reference:
🔍 New finding: cash purchases have no photo trigger
➡️ Narrow re-loop: new Empathize for that sub-problem
🚫 Not: restart the whole project

Why: a new finding scopes a fresh, narrow loop — it doesn't invalidate the parts of the process that already succeeded.
